summary: Defines a Robust Header Compression profile for IP/UDP/RTP packets that uses features of the lower layers to remove the header entirely for most packets in the best case. It extends the ROHC RTP profile. It is standards-track and obsoletes RFC 3242.

eli5.summary: Each package carries a long address label. If both ends already know it, the label can be skipped. This lets links leave it off most voice and video packets.

subtitle: A ROHC profile that, with help from the link layer, can send most real-time packets with no compressed header at all.

tldr.problem: Some older cellular air interfaces use radio bearers tuned to fixed payload sizes, so even one extra octet of ROHC header forces the next larger packet size, which is costly.
tldr.mechanism: The LLA profile adds a No-Header Packet: the compressed header is dropped entirely, and the link layer (the assisting layer) supplies what the header normally did, namely packet type, in-order delivery and loss indications.
tldr.outcome: For streams that suit it, most packets carry no header at all, and for other streams the profile behaves like ordinary ROHC RTP. It obsoletes RFC 3242 and has since been updated by RFC 4815.

today: RFC 4362 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3242 and has been updated by RFC 4815. The text itself leaves the link-specific details to other documents.

sections.title: Why Remove the Last Octet
sections.content:
Header compression shrinks the network and transport headers of a packet on each hop. ROHC (RObust Header Compression) was created because earlier schemes such as Compressed RTP degraded badly on wireless links with high error rates. ROHC RTP can already compress IP/UDP/RTP headers down to a total of one octet.

That one octet still matters on some links. Older air interfaces (the RFC names those based on GSM and IS-95) have radio bearers optimized for specific payload sizes, so adding even a single octet means using the next higher fixed packet size. The link-layer assisted (LLA) profile extends ROHC RTP (profile 0x0001) to give a header-free packet format for a certain application behavior, while staying fully transparent.

The RFC is clear that this is not about efficiency in general. It matches existing applications to existing link technologies, and the added complexity means it should only be used to optimize specific applications over specific links.
sections.eli5: On some old radio links, one extra byte makes the whole parcel jump to the next box size, which wastes a lot. This profile removes that last byte for most packets.

sections.title: How the Header Goes Away
sections.content:
The profile, identified as profile 0x0005, replaces the smallest and most frequent ROHC U/O-mode header (the one-octet header) with a no-header format. That header carried three things: a packet type identifier, the sequence number and a CRC. Each must be supplied some other way.

  • Packet type. The assisting layer MUST provide a way to tell packets with a header from packets without one.
  • Sequence number. The assisting layer MUST guarantee in-order delivery over the link and MUST give the receiver an indication of each packet loss, which lets the decompressor infer the sequence number. The RFC compares this to the principle behind VJ header compression.
  • CRC. Loss detection is already covered by those indications, and residual bit errors cannot damage a header that is never sent. To catch other errors, periodic context verification SHOULD be performed.

The profile cannot be used when the UDP checksum is enabled, which is always the case for IPv6/UDP. For IPv4/UDP the sender may disable the checksum. Where it is usable, LLA never has lower compression efficiency than ROHC RTP.
sections.eli5: The little label told three things: what kind of parcel, which number in the line, and a check code. The truck now promises the order and reports losses, so the label is not needed.

sections.title: The Three New Packet Types
sections.content:
The profile adds three packet types to those of ROHC RTP.

The No-Header Packet (NHP) consists only of the payload of the original packet. It MAY be used when all header fields are unchanged or follow the established change pattern, so only sequence information needs conveying. An LLA compressor is not allowed to deliver NHP packets in R-mode.

The Context Synchronization Packet (CSP) has packet type identifier 11111010, followed by a 2-octet RTP Payload Length and a ROHC header. The compressor drops the payload so that context can be kept in sync cheaply when the stream overruns the channel bandwidth. The payload length is included because the decompressor needs it to infer the IPv4 total length, the IPv6 payload length, the UDP length and the IPv4 header checksum. After processing a CSP, the decompressor MUST discard the packet.

The Context Check Packet (CCP) has packet type identifier 11111011 and carries no payload, only a C bit and a 7-bit CRC. With C=1 the CRC is valid and the decompressor is REQUIRED to verify its context with it, and a CCP with C=0 MUST be ignored. A CCP does not update context. It is useful when a synchronized physical link must send data at fixed intervals even though no compressed packet is available.
sections.eli5: There are three special parcels: one with no label, one that is only a label to keep both sides in step, and one that is just a small check note.

sections.title: The Assisting Layer and Safety Rules
sections.content:
The RFC defines the meaning of the interfaces between ROHC and the assisting layer, but not how to implement them. From compressor to assisting layer, everything except the NHP is always delivered, along with the RTP sequence number and segmentation flags. In the other direction, the decompressor MUST receive an indication of each packet loss for CID=0, and each received packet together with a flag saying whether it is an NHP.

Several rules protect against context damage:

  • Optimistic approach. Because an NHP has no CRC, the two sides must agree on how many updates are sent for a field change. If, for example, three consecutive updates are sent, the decompressor must invalidate its context if three or more consecutive physical packets are lost. Documents describing a link technology REQUIRED to define how this is agreed.
  • Fast initialization. The D bit of the IR packet is redefined: D=0 means no dynamic chain and that the payload was discarded. The packet is then discarded after processing.
  • CV-REQUEST. A feedback option (option type 8) the decompressor MAY use to ask for a context-verifying packet. The next packet SHOULD NOT then be sent as an NHP.
  • Periodic verification. Sending context-updating packets periodically is RECOMMENDED.
  • Context identifier. An NHP cannot carry a CID, so NHPs can only be used for CID=0.
sections.eli5: Both sides agree on the rules in advance: how often to double-check, what to do if parcels go missing, and that only one particular line of parcels may travel without labels.

sections.title: Implementation Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC suggests parameters in addition to those of ROHC RTP. At the compressor:

  • ALWAYS_PAD (boolean, default FALSE) makes every header packet carry at least one octet of ROHC padding, which can serve as a leading sequence that tells header packets from NHPs.
  • PREFERRED_PACKET_SIZES lists sizes the link prefers, each optionally restricted to NHP_ONLY or RHP_ONLY. NHPs can only be delivered if the payload size is in the list.
  • LARGE_PACKETS_ALLOWED (default TRUE) decides whether oversized packets are sent as is or split with ROHC segmentation.
  • VERIFICATION_PERIOD (default 0, meaning disabled) requires a packet with a CRC at least once every N packets.

At the decompressor, NHP_PACKET flags a packet as an NHP, PHYSICAL_PACKET_LOSS signals a packet lost on the link, and PRE_LINK_PACKET_LOSS signals a sequence gap not caused by a link error.

Link-specific details belong in other documents. Those documents MAY use the unused packet type pattern 11111001 for lower layer signaling.
sections.eli5: These are the dials and signals a builder can use: how big parcels are, when to pad, how often to check, and how to report a lost parcel.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of ROHC RTP apply, with one addition. An intruder who injects bogus CCP packets with random CRC values onto the link would make the CRC check fail at the decompressor for the wrong reason. That causes unnecessary context invalidation, feedback messages and refresh packets, which would greatly reduce the benefit of ROHC and of the extra efficiency this profile provides. The RFC notes that the same remarks about the presence of such an intruder apply.
sections.eli5: A troublemaker could throw fake check notes onto the truck, making the receiver think things went wrong and ask for lots of fresh labels.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 3242
sections.content:
This document replaces RFC 3242 to fix one technical flaw and clarify one implementation issue.

The flaw: the CSP format in RFC 3242 was non-interoperable when carrying a header with a 3-bit or 7-bit CRC, because the payload was dropped and the decompressor could not infer the payload-length-dependent fields. The fix is that the CSP now carries the length of the RTP payload.

The clarification: on CRC failure, the actions of Section 5.3.2.2.3 of the ROHC specification apply, but steps a through d only, since detecting sequence number wraparound and local repair do not apply when the failing packet is a CCP.
sections.eli5: The first rulebook had a mistake that stopped two builders' gear from working together. This version fixes it by adding the size of the missing contents to one kind of packet.

fields.name: Packet type
fields.desc: Packet type identifier for the CCP.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: 0 means the CRC field is not used; 1 means a valid CRC is present.

fields.name: CRC
fields.desc: 7-bit CRC over the original uncompressed header.
